paras.text: Claims Clocks and D I F S, Audio Lecture
This chapter turns Michigan insurance law into a calendar you can actually use on a real file.

If you remember nothing else from the next half hour, remember this one idea. Almost none of Michigan's claims clocks start by themselves. They start when a specific piece of paper reaches the insurance company. A notice of loss. A proof of loss. A written demand.

So here is the practical consequence, and it is the most valuable sentence in this chapter. If you wait for the carrier's own estimate before sending anything, you have handed it the calendar. Nothing is running. The carrier is under no pressure, because no paper started any clock.
That idea is the spine of everything below. Thirteen ideas. After most of them, a question and then silence. Answer out loud.
Idea one. Notice of loss, and a number that does not exist.

A loss happens. Under M C L five hundred point two eight three three, subsection one, letter l, every Michigan fire policy must contain, quote, the notification requirements when a loss occurs, end quote.
Now notice what that does not say. It does not say how many days the insured has to report. The day count lives in the policy's conditions section, not the statute.
So if someone asks how many days a homeowner has to report a loss under Michigan statute, the honest answer is that the statute sets no number. Read the policy.
That is worth saying confidently, because people will insist there is a statutory number. There is not.
Idea two. The insurer's thirty day duty, and a shortcut that is wrong.
Once that notice of loss lands on the insurer's desk, the insurer has its own clock running.

M C L five hundred point two zero zero six, subsection three, says the insurer shall specify in writing the materials that constitute a satisfactory proof of loss not later than thirty days after receipt of a claim, unless the claim is settled within those thirty days.

Read the trigger carefully. Thirty days from receipt of the claim itself, meaning the notice. Not from receipt of a proof of loss. So the moment a homeowner reports a loss, a thirty day clock starts on the insurer to tell her in writing exactly what documents it needs.

Now be careful, because there is a shortcut people repeat that is simply wrong. You will hear that if the insurer stays silent past day thirty, whatever proof of loss the homeowner later submits automatically counts as satisfactory, and that Griswold says so.
Griswold says the opposite. Whether a satisfactory proof of loss was received is a question of fact.

So do not build a strategy on that shortcut. But do not undervalue the duty either. It is a dated obligation the carrier either met or did not, and it locks in the document list the carrier said it needed. A carrier that later demands a pile of things it never listed has a problem.

That subsection has a second rule that is genuinely useful. If a proof of loss covers only part of the claim, that part is timely paid if paid within sixty days of receipt, and any later piece gets its own fresh sixty day clock.
That is why smart strategy splits a claim into the undisputed part and the fought over part. You get the clean money moving on its own clock instead of letting it sit hostage to the disputed part.
Question. Homeowner reports a fire on June first. What does the carrier owe her by roughly July first, and what does silence past that date NOT give her.

By roughly July first the carrier owes a written specification of the materials that constitute a satisfactory proof of loss, under two zero zero six, subsection three. Silence does not automatically make her later proof of loss satisfactory. Under Griswold that stays a question of fact.
Idea three. The mortgagee's sixty days, and what it is not.
A separate clock sits in the mortgagee clause.

Under M C L five hundred point two eight three three, subsection one, letter j, if a loss is payable to a named mortgagee and the insured fails to render a proof of loss, the insurer can notify the mortgagee, which then has sixty days after that notice to render its own.
Two limits on it. It only matters if the insured never submits her own. If she does, the mortgagee clock never turns on at all.
And do not confuse it with an insured's own proof of loss deadline. The statute sets none. Sixty days belongs to the mortgagee alone, as a backstop.
Idea four. The two money clocks, thirty and sixty, and the trap between them.
These are the two most confused clocks in the chapter. Two numbers, measuring different things.

The thirty day clock, in M C L five hundred point two eight three three, subsection one, letter p, and echoed in M C L five hundred point two eight three six, subsection two, says the loss is payable within thirty days after receipt of proof of the amount of loss. That is the payment deadline.

The sixty day clock is a different animal. It comes from M C L five hundred point two zero zero six, subsection four, and it governs when twelve percent simple interest starts piling up on unpaid benefits. From a date sixty days after satisfactory proof of loss was received, if the claimant is the insured or a person directly entitled to benefits.
Now here is the trap, and it is a good one. A claim paid on day forty five is late under the thirty day payment rule, but may owe zero interest, because interest does not start until day sixty one.
Lateness and interest are not the same thing. Say that back to yourself, because you will want to conflate them.

One more critical detail. The reasonably in dispute defense, which normally lets an insurer off the hook for an unfair trade practice, does not apply to this twelve percent when the claimant is a first party insured. It is written only into the sentence about third party tort claimants.

Two cases nail this down. Griswold Properties versus Lexington Insurance Company, two seventy six Michigan Appeals five fifty one, and Nickola versus M I C General Insurance Company, five hundred Michigan one fifteen, at the Supreme Court. Both hold a first party insured gets the twelve percent regardless of dispute.
And one honest boundary. No published Michigan property case extends that right to a restoration contractor holding an assignment of benefits. It belongs to the insured.
Question. Proof of the amount of loss lands March first, carrier pays April tenth. Late? Interest owed?

Late, yes, because payment was due within thirty days under letter p. Interest, no, because the twelve percent does not begin until sixty days after satisfactory proof of loss, which would be roughly April thirtieth.
Idea five. Appraisal, in one minute.
M C L five hundred point two eight three three, subsection one, letter m, has two key day counts. Twenty and fifteen.

After a written demand, each side has twenty days to name a competent, independent appraiser and tell the other side who it picked. Those two then try to agree on a neutral umpire. If they cannot within fifteen days, either party can ask a circuit judge, in the county where the loss occurred or the property sits, to pick one.
Whatever any two of those three sign off on in writing becomes the amount of the loss. Each side pays its own appraiser. The umpire's cost and other appraisal expenses split fifty fifty.

And remember what appraisal decides. Only the amount, never whether the loss is covered. That distinction comes from Auto Owners Insurance Company versus Kwaiser, one hundred ninety Michigan Appeals four hundred eighty two, where the court said flatly that the issue of coverage is for the court, not the appraisers.
Idea six. Cancellation, where two statutes stack.
This is where people get confused about which rule controls, so let me separate the layers.

M C L five hundred point two eight three three, subsection one, letter i, is the fire policy's own built in cancellation clause. The insurer can cancel at any time by mailing notice not less than ten days before cancellation, postage prepaid, tendering or promising to refund the excess earned premium.
Understand what that ten days is. It is the floor every fire policy must contain as a contract term. It is about what the policy must say.
For an actual homeowner's policy, that is not the end of it. The Essential Insurance Act, chapter twenty one, layers an effectiveness rule on top for what it calls home insurance.

M C L five hundred point two one two three says a termination is not effective unless the insurer mails written notice at least thirty days before the termination date. Except a notice given inside the policy's first fifty five days can be effective in as little as twenty days. And nonpayment notices follow whatever the policy itself says.
And termination is a defined word, at M C L five hundred point two one zero four, subsection five. A refusal to continue to insure for reasons other than nonpayment of premium.
That definition is why nonpayment sits outside the thirty day rule. It was never inside it, because nonpayment is not a termination as the act defines it.

So the pair to hold: ten days is what the fire policy must say, thirty days is when a home insurance termination becomes effective. Different statutes, different jobs. And twenty days inside the first fifty five.
Idea seven. The closed list, and a bulletin about satellite photos.
D I F S spells this out in bulletin twenty twenty five dash twelve dash I N S, on insurers using aerial imagery to assess roof condition.

It says that canceling or nonrenewing home insurance for reasons other than nonpayment triggers the thirty day rule, and that the reasons must come from the closed list in M C L five hundred point two one one seven.
Here is that closed list. Not being an eligible person. Physical condition and occupancy. A changed adjacent hazard. Claim history. And underinsurance.
Five grounds. That is the whole list, and closed means closed.

Now notice what is not on it. Cosmetic roof discoloration seen in a satellite photo. The bulletin says almost exactly that: mere cosmetic roof issues, like discoloration or streaking, are not valid grounds for cancellation or nonrenewal.
That is a genuinely useful thing to know for a homeowner who just got a nonrenewal notice after a drone or satellite sweep.
Idea eight. A stale number printed in a live statute.
On that claim history ground, here is a number that will catch you if you read only the statute.
The statute still prints three thousand and four thousand dollars as the three year paid claim minimums. Those are stale.
Subsection five tells the director to raise them with inflation every sixth year and certify the new figures in a bulletin, and bulletin twenty twenty four dash zero two dash I N S did exactly that.

Since January first, twenty twenty four, the real numbers are five thousand dollars excluding weather related claims and six thousand six hundred including them, with the next adjustment due in twenty thirty.

This is a classic superseded figure trap, and I want you to feel the shape of it, because it repeats all over insurance law. The statute is real. The number printed inside it is not current. If you quote three thousand and four thousand from the statute text, you are quoting something true on the page and false in the world.
Question. Claim history grounds. Which dollar figures are live, which are printed in the statute, and what reconciles them.

Live are five thousand dollars excluding weather related claims and six thousand six hundred including them, since January first twenty twenty four. The statute still prints three thousand and four thousand. Subsection five directs the director to adjust them every sixth year by bulletin, and bulletin twenty twenty four dash zero two dash I N S certified the current ones.
Idea nine. The one year suit clock, frozen.

M C L five hundred point two eight three three, subsection one, letter q, says an action under the policy must be commenced within one year after the loss, or within whatever longer period the policy itself specifies.
But that one year period is tolled, meaning the clock pauses, from the moment the insured notifies the insurer of the loss until the insurer formally denies liability.

Walk the dates. A loss January fifth, notice January sixth. If the insurer never formally denies, only that single day counts against the year. The clock stays frozen the whole time the claim sits open.
If a clear formal denial arrives six months later, the remaining days run again from that date.

Now the judgment call you will actually face. A partial payment with a reservation of rights is not, by itself, a formal denial. A letter saying the company considers the file closed reads much closer to one.

And the statute never defines formally denies. So here is the working rule: calendar every ambiguous letter as if it might be the one that restarts the clock. You cannot un-miss a deadline, and the cost of calendaring a letter that turned out to be harmless is nothing.
Idea ten. D I F S, and the three things it cannot do.

The Department of Insurance and Financial Services describes its Office of Consumer Services as providing consumer information, investigating complaints, and assisting consumers in resolving them whenever possible, after first encouraging people to try the carrier directly.
You can file online or by mail, email, or fax. The call center runs Monday through Friday, eight to five.
But here is the honest limit you need cold, and it is the difference between helping a homeowner and misleading one.

What D I F S says it does is investigate and help resolve. What its own bulletin twenty twenty five dash twenty five dash I N S says it can bring down on a carrier is fines, and suspension or revocation of the carrier's certificate of authority.
Now notice what is missing from all of that. Nothing D I F S publishes says it can decide whether your loss is covered, order a specific payment, or act as your attorney.
Do not promise a homeowner any of those three. That promise is how you lose someone's trust two months later.

And nowhere on that page does D I F S promise a number of days for its own response, or for forcing a carrier to answer. So if someone tells you D I F S makes carriers answer within thirty days, that is not supported by anything D I F S publishes.

One more piece of realism. The statute behind the enforcement, section twenty twenty six, reaches conduct other than isolated incidents showing a persistent tendency. So one badly handled file is not by itself the violation.
Idea eleven. Young, and the one line that divides the remedies.

Young versus Michigan Mutual Insurance Company holds an insured has no independent cause of action under section twenty twenty six, the fourteen unfair practices, because that section exists to give the regulator authority over continuing practices.
But the same case approves a private suit to recover the interest penalty under section twenty zero six.
So memorize the split in one line. The twelve percent you can sue for. The fourteen practices you cannot.
Idea twelve. The quiet statute that makes a complaint letter worth writing.
A quieter statute works in the background, and it is one almost nobody uses on purpose.

M C L five hundred point two zero two six, subsection two. It is an unfair practice for an insurer to fail to keep a complete record of every insured complaint since its last examination, with the total count, classification by line, the nature of each, its disposition, and the time it took to process.

Think about what that means for you practically. A certified letter of complaint straight to the carrier, even before or instead of D I F S, creates a paper trail the company must log. It goes into a record a regulator will eventually read.
That is a low cost move with real downstream weight, and most people never make it.
Idea thirteen. Two things outside the Insurance Code that decide when money actually arrives.
First, the mortgage servicer, which is often the real reason a homeowner is still waiting.

If a homeowner's mortgage is owned by Fannie Mae, the check usually goes to the servicer first, because of the mortgagee clause. Fannie Mae's Servicing Guide, section B dash five dash zero one, Insured Loss Events, tells servicers how to release it.

If the loan is current or less than thirty one days behind, the servicer can release an initial payment up to the greater of forty thousand dollars, thirty three percent of total proceeds, or whatever exceeds the loan's remaining balance plus interest and advances. Then the rest in draws tied to repair inspections.

If the loan is thirty one days or more behind, the rules tighten. Small proceeds of five thousand dollars or less can go out in one payment. But anything larger gets an initial release of only twenty five percent of the proceeds, capped at the greater of ten thousand dollars or the amount above the loan payoff, with the rest released in twenty five percent increments after inspections and a required final inspection.
And critically for anyone in this business: servicers must prohibit paying a public adjuster or other third party fee out of proceeds unless Fannie Mae approves it in writing first.

Now label what that is. A private investor rule, not Michigan law. It binds the servicer, not the insurer. And it is often exactly why a homeowner wins the statutory thirty day payment fight and still waits weeks for cash. The carrier obeyed the statute. The servicer is following a different rulebook.

Second, understand what a D I F S bulletin is legally. Not a statute. It is the director's interpretive guidance on how D I F S reads and enforces the Insurance Code, replaceable by the next bulletin with no legislative vote.

That cuts both ways, and this is the subtle part. A bulletin can also be the only place a statutory number's live version lives, as with the five thousand and six thousand six hundred figures you just learned. Not law, and yet the only current source for a number the law relies on.
Three live bulletins to keep straight.

Bulletin twenty twenty four dash twenty six dash I N S says that starting with homeowners and dwelling policies issued or renewed on or after July first, twenty twenty five, an insurer depreciating what it calls nontangible items, meaning labor, taxes, fees, and overhead and profit, in actual cash value must do it through a separate, optional, lower premium endorsement naming those items, rather than burying it in policy definitions. That conditions the practice. It does not ban it.

Bulletin twenty twenty five dash twenty five dash I N S says dragging out claims administration or making unreasonable proof of loss demands to gain leverage violates the Code, citing section twenty twenty six. But it is written around auto claims, not property.

And bulletin twenty twenty six dash sixteen dash I N S sets the fire insurance maximum escrow under M C L five hundred point two two two seven at twenty five thousand ninety dollars for July first, twenty twenty six through June thirtieth, twenty twenty seven. Do not confuse it with the separate calendar year escrow under M C L five hundred point two eight four five, which bulletin twenty twenty five dash twenty seven dash I N S sets at sixteen thousand three hundred eighty three dollars for twenty twenty six.
Two provisions, two amounts, two periods. That is the whole distinction.
Time for the recap. Fast, as a self check.

Notice starts the insurer's thirty day duty to specify proof of loss requirements, and starts tolling the one year suit clock. Proof of the amount of loss starts two clocks: thirty days to pay, sixty days before twelve percent interest begins. An amount dispute can go to appraisal, twenty days to name an appraiser, fifteen more to agree on an umpire. Fire policy cancellation needs at least ten days notice, but a home insurance cancellation or nonrenewal for reasons other than nonpayment needs at least thirty, tied to the closed list in section twenty one one seven, whose claim history dollars are five thousand and six thousand six hundred, not the three thousand and four thousand printed in the statute. And the suit clock sits frozen from notice until a formal denial arrives.
Master that sequence and you have mastered this chapter. If any of the questions I asked gave you trouble, that is exactly where to drill.
